clinicalPearls: Postpartum haemorrhage is excessive bleeding after birth; primary PPH occurs within the first 24 hours and secondary PPH from 24 hours up to about 12 weeks postpartum
The causes are usefully remembered as the four Ts: tone (uterine atony), trauma (genital tract lacerations), tissue (retained placenta or products), and thrombin (coagulopathy)
Uterine atony is by far the commonest cause, so uterine massage and uterotonic agents are first-line alongside resuscitation
Active management of the third stage of labour with a prophylactic uterotonic reduces the incidence and severity of PPH
Blood loss is frequently underestimated visually, so vital signs, quantitative assessment, and a high index of suspicion are essential

A structured stepwise escalation moves from uterotonics to mechanical measures (bimanual compression, balloon tamponade) and then to surgical options such as compression sutures, vessel ligation, or hysterectomy
Tranexamic acid given early reduces death from bleeding and should be administered promptly
Early involvement of senior obstetric, anaesthetic, and haematology teams with activation of a massive transfusion protocol improves outcomes
reference.pathophysiology: Normal postpartum haemostasis depends on vigorous myometrial contraction that mechanically compresses the spiral arteries of the placental bed, supported by the clotting cascade. Postpartum haemorrhage results when one or more of these mechanisms fail: the uterus fails to contract (atony, often from overdistension, prolonged or augmented labour, infection, or retained tissue); vessels are torn by genital tract trauma; retained placental tissue or invasive placentation prevents effective contraction; or coagulation is impaired by dilution, consumption, or a pre-existing disorder. Ongoing loss can precipitate hypovolaemic shock and a self-perpetuating coagulopathy.
additionalDifferentials: Genital tract trauma including cervical or vaginal lacerations and haematomas
Retained placenta or retained products of conception
Inherited or acquired coagulopathy including disseminated intravascular coagulation
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative measurement of blood loss and continuous vital sign monitoring
Full blood count and serial haemoglobin
Group and cross-match with early activation of transfusion support
Examination under anaesthesia and ultrasound to identify retained tissue or genital tract trauma
redFlags: Tachycardia, hypotension, and other signs of hypovolaemic shock
Continued brisk bleeding despite uterotonics and uterine massage
Clinical or laboratory evidence of coagulopathy
A high uterine fundus with a boggy uterus indicating atony, or a suddenly inverted uterus
Suspected placenta accreta spectrum after a difficult placental delivery
reference.prognosis: With prompt recognition, resuscitation, and stepwise treatment most women recover fully. Delay in diagnosis or treatment can lead to shock, organ failure, need for hysterectomy with loss of fertility, and death; postpartum haemorrhage remains one of the leading causes of maternal mortality worldwide, particularly in low-resource settings.
pitfalls: Underestimating blood loss by visual assessment alone
Failing to recognise ongoing bleeding masked by the physiological cardiovascular reserve of pregnancy until late collapse
Not systematically excluding retained tissue and genital tract trauma when atony seems controlled but bleeding persists
Delaying tranexamic acid and blood product replacement
Escalating too slowly to mechanical and surgical measures when medical therapy fails
